Ralph Ellison. The novelist best known for Invisible Man, a masterwork of modernist literature that explored Black identity and existence in mid-twentieth-century America through an unnamed protagonist's journey from South to North. His work synthesized jazz rhythms, folk traditions, and high modernism into a vision of American racial experience.

Invisible Man, published in 1952, became a defining novel of American letters. It uses the metaphor of invisibility—the protagonist unseen by white America despite his physical presence—to describe the Black experience in America. The novel opens in an underground room lit by thirteen hundred sixty-nine light bulbs, establishing a surreal, symbolically charged setting that combines homelessness with philosophical depth. Ellison drew heavily on American vernacular traditions, folk stories, and jazz idiom, making his prose rhythmic and sonically inventive while addressing modernist themes.

His essays, including one called Harlem Is Nowhere, reflected on the cultural and psychological dimensions of racism and segregation with sociological depth. He spent decades working on a second novel, Juneteenth, which was published posthumously in 1999, demonstrating his uncompromising artistic standards. He engaged with questions of literary craft and American cultural identity in essays and interviews, positioning himself as both artist and intellectual. Like James Baldwin, his contemporary, Ellison grappled with similar themes of American identity and racial consciousness, bringing modernist sophistication to the urgent question of what it means to be Black in America.
